checkpoints: CPU sitting near 0% while a large backlog barely drains is the signature of an I/O-bound workload, not a CPU-bound one — each job spends nearly all its wall-clock time parked on an `await` for a network round-trip rather than doing computation.

At `concurrency: 1`, a BullMQ worker only ever has one job in flight, so the per-job network latency accumulates serially across the whole backlog — total drain time is roughly job count multiplied by per-job latency.

Raising worker concurrency lets multiple jobs be in flight on the same single-threaded event loop at once: while job A is suspended awaiting its I/O call, the loop is free to start job B's request, then job C's, so N one-second I/O waits overlap and finish in roughly one second instead of N seconds.

The speedup comes purely from interleaving idle wait time, not from added CPU parallelism — which is why the same change would not help, and could even hurt, a CPU-bound job like image resizing or hashing, since that work actually occupies the single JS thread instead of waiting on I/O.

Concurrency has a real ceiling set by downstream resources: pushing it past the size of a connection pool (database or SMTP) just queues the extra jobs waiting for a free connection, so real throughput caps at the pool size no matter how high concurrency is configured.

Pushing concurrency past a downstream provider's rate quota manufactures failed requests such as HTTP 429s, and the retries triggered by those failures can eat up whatever throughput gain the higher concurrency produced.

A safe concurrency value is sized to roughly the minimum of the connection-pool size and available quota headroom, with a queue-level rate limiter (for example `limiter: { max, duration }`) enforcing the hard quota explicitly instead of letting workers discover it by failing.

The right way to size concurrency is empirical rather than guessed: measure drain time and queue stats at several concurrency values, watch for connection-wait time and error responses as concurrency rises, and stop increasing at the knee of the curve where throughput stops improving and errors start climbing.
